etymology: Hebrew yether, “abundance” or “remainder, that which excels,” a name borne by several men of Scripture, here noted in the genealogy of Judah.
biblical_def: Jether is a name borne by several men in the sacred record, and one of them stands in the genealogy of Judah which the Chronicler kept as a treasure of the LORD’s faithfulness to that tribe (1Ch 4:17). The name itself signifies “abundance” or “that which excels,” and the same word names Jether the firstborn of Gideon, a youth so afraid that he would not draw his sword when his father bade him slay the kings (Jdg 8:20), and Jether the father of Amasa, kinsman of David. The dictionary does not labour to untangle every Jether, but it honours that the Spirit of God thought it good to write these names in the book. Every name in them, even the obscure Jether of whom we know little more than his place in the line, was kept by the providence of God toward the promise. He who numbered the hairs of our heads numbered also the sons of Judah, that not one should be lost out of the record of His covenant mercy. etymology: Hebrew mesha‘, perhaps “deliverance” or “retreat,” the firstborn of Caleb in the genealogy of Judah, father of Ziph.
biblical_def: Mesha is named as the firstborn of Caleb in the Chronicler’s genealogy of the tribe of Judah, the father of Ziph and reckoned in the house of the Calebites (1Ch 2:42). His name is to be distinguished from Mesha king of Moab, who rebelled against Israel; this Mesha is a man of the covenant line, not the rebel of the moabite stone. Of his deeds the Scripture records nothing beyond his place as firstborn and his fathering of Ziph, a name that became a town of the wilderness of Judah where David hid from Saul. The dictionary does not invent a history for a man held in such honourable silence; it marks that the Spirit of God set down the firstborn of Caleb’s house, the firstfruits of that line. The firstborn in Israel was a thing of weight, claimed by the LORD as His own and figuring the Firstborn among many brethren who should come, even Christ. Mesha stands therefore in a line that points beyond itself to the great Firstborn from the dead. He is a witness that the providence of God reckons the generations one by one, the firstborn and the least alike, and that a man known only as a son and a father is yet kept for ever in the record of God’s faithful keeping of the line of Judah.

etymology: Hebrew chelets, perhaps “strength” or “loins,” one of David’s mighty men, called the Paltite or the Pelonite of the children of Ephraim.
biblical_def: Helez is numbered among the mighty men of David, that famed company of valiant soldiers who stood with the king through his wars and his wanderings (2Sa 23:26). He is called the Paltite in the book of Samuel and the Pelonite in the Chronicler’s parallel list, and he is reckoned of the children of Ephraim, set over a course of the army in the seventh month, of four and twenty thousand men (1Ch 27:10). Of his particular exploits the Scripture is silent, yet to be written among David’s mighty men is honour enough, for these were the men who hazarded their lives for their lord and helped to establish his kingdom. The dictionary marks that Helez served faithfully in his appointed course, neither first nor most renowned of the thirty, but steadfast in his place month by month. There is a pattern of grace here, for the kingdom of David is a figure of the kingdom of great David’s greater Son, and the men who held their rank in his host are an image of those who serve Christ each in his own order. Helez stands as a witness that faithfulness in an assigned station, though it win no song of its own, is honoured by the LORD; for it is required in stewards that a man be found faithful, and the good and faithful servant shall hear his Master’s Well done.

etymology: Hebrew zabad, “gift” or “endowed,” a son of Ahlai of the line of Sheshan, reckoned among the mighty men of David.
biblical_def: Zabad the son of Ahlai is named both in the Chronicler’s genealogy of Judah, where he descends through Sheshan by way of his daughter and the Egyptian servant Jarha, and among the valiant men of David’s host (1Ch 2:36; 1Ch 11:41). His name signifies “gift,” a fitting word for one whose very lineage was a token of the LORD’s mercy, for Sheshan had no sons but daughters, and the line was preserved through a servant given a place in the house. Of Zabad’s own exploits the Scripture is silent, yet he is written among the mighty men who upheld David’s kingdom. The dictionary honours that the providence of God preserved this branch of Judah when it seemed it must fail, and brought forth from it a man counted worthy of the king’s company. There is gospel here, for the LORD delights to graft the unlikely and the stranger into His house and to make of them gifts to His people. Zabad stands as a witness that no failing line is beyond the mercy of God to preserve, and that a name meaning gift is rightly borne by a man whom grace, and not natural succession, set among the valiant. The good and faithful servant, though sprung of a servant’s seed, is honoured in the record of the LORD.

etymology: Hebrew meshelemyahu, “whom the LORD recompenses” or “the LORD repays,” a Korhite porter and chief of the gatekeepers of the house of the LORD.
biblical_def: Meshelemiah was a Korhite, a son of Kore of the sons of Asaph, appointed among the porters or gatekeepers of the house of the LORD in the ordering of the temple service under David (1Ch 26:1). He had sons and brethren, able men for strength for the service, and lots were cast for every gate, that each ward might be kept in its course. His name signifies “whom the LORD recompenses,” a fitting name for one whose office was to stand at the doors of the sanctuary, keeping the thresholds of the house of God. The porter’s work was lowly in the eyes of men, neither priest nor singer, yet the psalmist counted it the highest honour, saying he had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of his God than dwell in the tents of wickedness. The dictionary honours Meshelemiah as a steward of the gates, set to guard the holy place against defilement and to admit the worshippers in their order. There is grace here for all who serve in humble station, for the threshold of God’s house is a more blessed place than the palaces of the ungodly. Meshelemiah stands as a witness that the LORD recompenses His faithful doorkeepers, and that to keep the gate of the sanctuary is no mean calling, but a service the LORD Himself ordained and will reward.

etymology: Hebrew shebu’el, “captive of God” or “return ye to God,” a son of Gershom the son of Moses, made ruler of the treasures of the house of the LORD.
biblical_def: Shebuel was a son of Gershom, the son of Moses the man of God, and was set as ruler over the treasures of the house of the LORD in the ordering of the Levites under David (1Ch 23:16; 1Ch 26:24). His name signifies “captive of God” or, by another reading, “return ye to God,” and he is also called Shubael in the Chronicler’s record. It is a marvel of grace that a grandson of Moses should hold so quiet an office, a keeper of the treasuries, when his grandfather had stood upon the mount with God and led Israel out of Egypt; yet the line of Moses was not given the priesthood, but a Levite’s service among the rest. The dictionary honours that Shebuel was found faithful in the charge of the sacred treasures, neither grasping at greatness nor despising his lesser station. There is a lesson against pride of descent, for the seed of the greatest of the prophets served in the storehouse, and was content. To be a trusted steward of the LORD’s house is honour enough, for it is required in stewards that a man be found faithful. Shebuel stands as a witness that the LORD assigns to each his own ministry, that high birth gives no claim to high place, and that the faithful keeper of the treasure shall hear the Master’s Well done as surely as the prophet who led the people.
